t: Minimum Sum of Mountain Triplets II
o: A mountain triplet needs i<j<k with nums[i] < nums[j] > nums[k], minimizing the sum. Brute force over triples is O(n^3), too slow for n = 1e5. The key realization: for a fixed peak j, the best triplet uses the smallest valid element to its left and the smallest valid element to its right, both computable with prefix/suffix minimum scans. In [8,6,1,5,3], peak j=3 has left-min 1 and right-min 3, giving 9.
k: Prefix minimums give the smallest left wing; suffix minimums give the smallest right wing.
For peak j only pre[j-1] < nums[j] and suf[j+1] < nums[j] produce a valid triplet.

a.i: Build pre[i] = min(nums[0..i]) and suf[i] = min(nums[i..n-1]). For each interior index j as the peak, if pre[j-1] < nums[j] and suf[j+1] < nums[j], candidate sum = pre[j-1] + nums[j] + suf[j+1]. Taking the min over all j is optimal because smaller wings never hurt validity.
s: Compute prefix minima left to right and suffix minima right to left.
For each j in 1..n-2, check both strict inequalities against the wings.
Accumulate the minimum valid sum; output -1 if none exists.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over the array.
a.sp: O(n) for the prefix and suffix arrays (reducible to O(1) extra with a running suffix min scanned backwards).

w: This is the standard optimal solution; mention the monotonic-stack alternative only if asked about counting mountains rather than minimizing. Pitfall: inequalities must be strict (<, not <=), and remember the -1 case for arrays like [6,5,4,3,4,5].
